source.title: Provable Generalization of SGD-trained Neural Networks of Any Width in the Presence of Adversarial Label Noise
source.authors: Spencer Frei; Yuan Cao; Quanquan Gu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes and experimentally evaluates SGD generalization under adversarial label noise, using test classification error relative to the best halfspace. It does not reproduce the random-label fitting experiments in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions fitting random labels only when citing prior work; that cited result is not a row. Its own experiments report test accuracy as OPTlin varies, but do not report training error on random labels.
record.test_reason: The study investigates population classification error under adversarial label noise, rather than training-set memorization. It neither measures random-label fitting nor compares learning of clean and noisy labels over time. Figure 1b varies deterministic label flips with fixed 10% random noise outside the flipped region; this is not V4's random-corruption sweep. The record's T2 classification and V4 tested status should therefore be corrected.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate, but the formal guarantees need qualification: the authors prove existence of a competitive SGD iterate, with error of order Õ(√OPTlin) under anti-concentration and Õ(γ0⁻¹OPTlin) under a hard margin. The baseline experiments track the best linear classifier; architectural modifications and a different distribution can yield substantially better performance. These findings do not demonstrate random-label memorization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies generalization under adversarial label noise, rather than fitting completely random labels; it uses theoretical bounds and experiments on a two-dimensional Gaussian-mixture task.
record.method_sensitivity: For bias-free one-hidden-layer networks on the main experimental distribution, test accuracy is described as essentially unchanged across tested learning rates, initialization variances, and online versus multiple-pass SGD. With trainable biases and second-layer weights, the result depends strongly on initialization variance. The four-layer network performs closer to the Bayes classifier.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 2.6 and Corollaries 2.7–2.8 guarantee an SGD iterate with population error bounded relative to OPTlin under distributional assumptions, without explicit regularization. These are generalization guarantees, not guarantees of training-set memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Online SGD can find one-hidden-layer leaky-ReLU networks with population error controlled by the best halfspace's error under specified distributional assumptions, for arbitrary width and first-layer initialization.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4 and Figure 1b report test accuracy approximately equal to 1 − OPTlin for OPTlin ≤ 0.30 and slightly higher thereafter. Models are selected by validation error; no training-fit result is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On the tested Gaussian-mixture distributions with adversarial and random label noise, validation-selected bias-free one-hidden-layer networks generalize approximately as well as the best linear classifier.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix B reports near-Bayes performance with suitable initialization when biases and second-layer weights are trainable, and with a deeper network. Figure 10 also shows nonlinear learning beyond the best halfspace on a different distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization beyond linear classifiers depends on the distribution, architecture, and initialization in these experiments.

record.problems: The main experimental accuracy trend is shown in figures rather than given as a numerical table. Experiments use a specific two-dimensional Gaussian-mixture distribution; they do not measure training-set fit on random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the paper's reported outcomes do not directly measure any listed version. Figure 1b reports test accuracy as OPTlin varies, but does not establish the training-fit or random-label conditions named by V4.

untested.parts: All parts: fitting completely random training labels, near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence slowdown as random corruption increases.
Training-set fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit throughout a random-corruption sweep and steadily increasing test error toward chance. OPTlin is not the fraction of randomly corrupted labels, and training error is not reported.

Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them alone worsens generalization on true labels. Unregularized generalization under the paper's noise distributions does not establish these comparisons.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels and how their learning trajectories differ. An existence guarantee for a competitive SGD iterate does not establish this ordering.

record.verdict_notes: Keeping the row list empty is appropriate. The random-label capacity discussion cites prior work and supplies motivation; it is not an original fitting result or a challenge to V1. The related test-accuracy findings are already declared in rows_left_out, so no missing claim-bearing rows are required.

versions.untested_parts: Whether these networks fit completely random training labels, attain chance test error, or do so without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time relative to true labels and convergence as the fraction of corrupted labels increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The experiments vary OPTlin using a mixture of deterministic adversarial label noise and fixed-rate random classification noise, rather than sweeping the fraction of randomly corrupted labels from none to all. They report test accuracy, not perfect training fit.

The paper uses vanilla SGD without explicit regularization and reports generalization under adversarial label noise, but does not test fitting random labels or compare regularized and unregularized models on the stated outcomes.
The paper does not measure the order in which real patterns and noisy labels are learned.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The introduction discusses random-label fitting as motivation; the study does not test it or use it as a tool.

tranche.reason: Theorems and experiments concern population classification error under adversarial label noise, not random-label memorization or the other listed versions.

source_check.notes: The guarantees establish existence of a competitive SGD iterate, not convergence to an interpolating solution. Appendix B selects experimental checkpoints by validation error; training and test data share the noisy distribution.
